newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end higher after Greenspan's remarks.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end higher after Greenspan's remarks.

text.p: NEW YORK, Jan 21 ( Reuter) - U.S. Treasuries rebounded from early losses to close higher as players covered short positions following a relatively soothing speech by Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan, analysts said.
The 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended up 17/32 at 96-11/32 to yield 6.79 percent, the lowest since Janaury 15.

Experts said Greenspan's comments to the Senate Budget Committee on Tuesday delivered an upbeat assessment of the economy, but indicated few signs of imbalances or inflationary tensions associated with the end of past expansions.

"As long as the chairman doesn't see inflationy tensions, he's not willing to tighten (monetary policy). If he's not willing to tighten, don't be short," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
Some Wall Street experts had expected Greenspan would paint a bleaker inflation outlook during his testimony.

After the speech, the overall sentiment in the market was that some erosion on bullish conditions for the bond market might be noticed in the upcoming months. But the deterioration was not expected to be threatening enough to spark a major sell-off of bonds and a shoot up in long-term interest rates.

"That sentiment brought those investors who had gone short before the testimony back to the market. Greenspan's remarks were somewhat worrisome but not threatening," said a trader at a major foreign investment bank here.
"People were relieved after the speech," the trader added.

Greenspan said labor markets are "exceptionally tight" but noted it has not led to accelarated wages or inflation. He added the Fed will watch wages for signs of inflation but is not interested in "fine-tuning" the employment market.
Some hedge funds were seen buying selectively in the long end of the yield curve after the Fed chairman's testimony.
Scattered retail buying was also noticed, dealers said.
"It looks like there's some cash to be put to work at these levels," said a trader at a large U.S. bank. A strong dollar in New York also bolstered the Treasury market.
Pundits said, however, mounting concerns about upcoming supply was expected to wipe out the sense of relief the market enjoyed on Tuesday.

"I think caution will be the word ahead of the auctions because it seems fairly unlikely that much good news will be forthcoming any time soon," said Lee Youngdahl, vice-president at Aubrey G. Lanston and Co. Inc.

The Treasury will offer $17.5 billion in two-year notes on Wednesday, followed by $12.5 billion in five-year notes on Thursday. On top of that, the Treasury will dump on the market $7.0 billion in 10-year inflation-indexed notes on January 29.
Heavy corporate bond issuance has also been putting a lid on the market as well, analysts said.
On Tuesday, the market also took in a 0.2 percent rise in the seasonally adjusted BTM/Schroders weekly chain store sales index for the week ended January 18.

The two-year note closed up 1/32 at 99-20/32, yielding 5.96 percent. The five-year note traded up 3/32 at 99-10/32 to yield 6.29 percent. The ten-year note closed up 9/32 at 99-29/32, yielding 6.51 percent.
Later in the day, players also learned the Lynch, Jones & Ryan Inc. Redbook Retail Sales Index rose 0.3 percent in the first two weeks of fiscal January versus December.
Still on Tuesday, the market absorbed $23.1 billion in three- and six-months Treasury bills, which were placed at rates of 5.03 percent and 5.11 percent, respectively.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed flat at 5.03 percent. The six-month bill rate fell one basis point to 5.10 percent. The year bill rate was down two points at 5.27 percent.
